2	
3	Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson and then runs this same skill over its **own** additions before landing them, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted — and that has already survived at least one of those upgrade passes.
4	
5	**Weekly, deliberately.** Fresh prose is handled the night it is written, so what reaches this sweep is a slow-moving corpus; a daily re-read of it spent an opus dispatch and an owner-gated PR on a backlog that had not changed.
6	
7	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
8	
9	The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).
10	
11	## The method lives in the skill
12	
13	The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.
14	
15	## What a run does
16	
17	1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that govern **how we work** (not what the product does — see the skill's first gate), that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert), and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
18	2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. 21	
22	## What this task must never do
23	
24	- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
25	- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.

29

50	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
51	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
52

54	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
55	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
56	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
57	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
58	
59	**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
60	— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
61	answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
62	where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.
63

65	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.

68	
69	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
70	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
71	
72	> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the

74	> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.
75

77	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).

79	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
80	   doesn't ship.
81	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
82	   directional by kind.
83	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
84	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.

86	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
87	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
88	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's

90	check to the same fixture bar.

92	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
93	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.

96	
97	Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
98	deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
99	paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
100	how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
101	the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
102	either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.
103	
104	Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
105	activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
106	carries.

110	encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states

112	that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant

116

2

4	`chrome.tts`, `speechSynthesis`, the mic capture behind them). The mechanical rules — completion
5	handlers, mic release, which constraints a mic capture may even ask for, whether an error mapping
6	is total, and whether interim hypotheses are gated before delivery — are this pack's six checks;

8	
9	Each rule below is a judgment about the API, and holds for any voice-driven app. Where one cites
10	this repo — a file, a decision record, a measured number — that is the **evidence** it was drawn
11	from, not the scope it applies to; a rule grounded in a real instance beats one asserted in the
12	abstract. The measured values (the pause window especially) are this product's and should be
13	re-measured elsewhere, not copied.
14	
15	The one thing to keep in mind everywhere below: **speech failures are silent**. Nothing throws,
16	nothing logs, the UI keeps showing a live session — the user just hears nothing, or is heard by
17	nobody. Design each of these surfaces so every path produces exactly one observable outcome.
18	
19	## Where each API can run

22	  recognition needs a document, and the mic grant belongs to nytimes.com), so speaking is a
23	  relay: the content script sends `cc:speak` over the long-lived `cc-session` port and the

25	  `speech/tts-port.js` so the orchestrator can't tell the difference. Prefer `chrome.tts` over
26	  `speechSynthesis` because it is immune to the page's autoplay rules (decision D2).

30	`webkitSpeechRecognition` **owns its own capture and exposes no hook for
31	`MediaTrackConstraints`** — you cannot ask the recognizer for echo cancellation. Chrome applies
32	its default AEC (a loopback of playout audio) to that capture, which already attenuates
33	`speechSynthesis`, but it misses `chrome.tts`'s OS-rendered output. So the residual echo is
34	handled at the app level by a string-match echo guard (REQ-SPCH-005), and that is the design,
35	not a stopgap (decision D11).
36	
37	Two traps around this:
38	
39	- `suppressLocalAudioPlayback` and `restrictOwnAudio` read like the fix for this and are not:
40	  they are **`getDisplayMedia` screen-capture** constraints, filtering a captured tab's own
41	  playout out of that tab's track, and `getUserMedia` ignores them without a word. The cost of
42	  reaching for one is not the dead property — it is that the echo guard that would have worked
43	  never gets written. (Enforced by the `mic-constraints-not-screen-capture` check.)
44	- The constraints you *can* set (`echoCancellation`, `noiseSuppression`, `autoGainControl`)
45	  apply only to the one capture you own — the permission preflight. Their real value there is
46	  diagnostic: read `track.getSettings().echoCancellation` back and log it. Whether AEC actually
47	  engaged on this device is the single most useful fact when diagnosing a self-echo report, and
48	  it is the reason the session log carries `aec1`/`aec0` (`dev/docs/SESSION-LOG.md`).
49	
50	## Ask for the microphone in a moment you chose
51	
52	Surface the permission prompt deliberately, with a short warm-up `getUserMedia` — not as a side
53	effect of the first listen cycle. Two rules for that preflight:
54	
55	- **Run it even when permission is already granted.** Otherwise the device is only warmed, and
56	  AEC engagement only known, on the very first grant.
57	- **Retry once bare when the constrained call rejects.** A rejection is either a real denial or
58	  a browser balking at the constraint shape; only a second failure is a genuine denial. Reading
59	  a constraint quirk as "mic denied" ends the session for no reason.
60	
61	(The capture must then be released on every path — that is the `mic-capture-released` check.)
62	
63	## Endpointing is unreliable — plan for the miss
64	
65	Chrome decides on its own when an utterance ended, and it does get it wrong: interim hypotheses
66	keep arriving and no final result ever lands. Left alone the user repeats themselves and you get
67	`"heart heart"`. The fix is a pause monitor that discards the half-heard input and reopens a
68	fresh cycle — with interim results used **only** as the "still speaking" signal, never delivered
69	to the caller. (That last half is the `stt-interim-results-gated` check; the monitor itself, and
70	the window below, are yours.)
71	
72	Tune the window from real sessions, not from taste: 1.2 s cut real commands off solvers who
73	paused to think mid-instruction; 1.8 s keeps only the genuine missed-endpoint case. Anything
74	that ships an audible cue for the reset needs the same care — it fires often.
75	
76	## Contextual biasing exists only on the on-device path
77	
78	`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` / `processLocally` work only where Chrome has an on-device model.
79	Treat biasing as strictly best-effort:
80	
81	- probe availability **once** and memoize the promise;
82	- accept only the literal `'available'` — never trigger a language-pack download;
83	- apply phrases inside a `try` and fall through to un-biased recognition on any failure;
84	- keep the un-biased path byte-for-byte unchanged (don't make every caller await a probe it
85	  doesn't need);
86	- and **record whether biasing actually engaged**, because recognition data from a session where
87	  it silently didn't says nothing about biasing.
88	
89	## Voices load lazily, and the default one is usually the worst
90	
91	`getVoices()` returning an empty list means *"not ready yet"*, not *"no voices"* — resolve the
92	voice on first speak and, on an empty list, use the default and try again next time rather than
93	caching the empty answer. The OS default is often the most robotic voice installed, so carry an
94	ordered preference list and take the first installed match. That list is **taste, and taste has
95	been wrong here before** (`Google US English` led it, sounded bad, and was demoted): treat both
96	the voice order and the speaking rate as user-facing settings with a modest default, not as
97	constants to tune once.
98	
99	## Give recognition errors a taxonomy
100	
101	Map the raw Web Speech error names onto a small named set the dialog policy can reason about,
102	and keep the mapping in one place. The policy cares about *kinds* — nothing heard, the mic was
103	refused, we aborted on purpose, the network went — not about spellings, and a `default → other`
104	arm means a browser inventing a new name degrades instead of crashing. (That the mapping is
105	total is the `stt-error-map-has-default` check; choosing the kinds, and keeping them in one
106	place, is not.) Log the codes short (`en`/`ed`/`ea`…) so a whole session fits in a diagnostics
107	dump.

1	# Adapting to a host page — the judgment core
2	
3	Working inside a web app you do not own: reading its DOM, driving it with synthetic input,
4	watching it change, and putting your own UI into its chrome. The mechanical rules — that a
5	page observer is disconnected, that a synthetic input event bubbles — are this pack's two
6	checks; what follows is only what no check can decide for you.
7	
8	Each rule below is a judgment about being a guest in someone else's page, and holds for any
9	code that does it — a userscript, an automation layer, an extension's content script. Where
10	one cites this repo — a file, a requirement id, a date — that is the **evidence** it was drawn
11	from, not the scope it applies to.
12	
13	The premise underneath all of it: **the host will change its markup without telling you, and
14	your code will not throw when it does.** A selector that matches nothing returns null; a click
15	on a renamed button never happens. Every rule here is about making that failure loud, local,
16	and cheap to fix.
17	
18	## Quarantine the host's DOM knowledge in one module
19	
20	All of it, behind an interface expressed in your own vocabulary — here `page-adapter/` returns
21	a `Snapshot` and takes `enterAnswer`, and the crossword model, the dialog policy and the
22	matcher never learn that the page exists (REQ-PAGE-011, `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §2). Two
23	things follow, and both are worth the discipline:
24	
25	- A redesign is a **one-directory** change, and the blast radius is knowable before you start.
26	- The rest of the codebase becomes testable without a browser at all — the pure layers here
27	  (`puzzle-model/`, `matching/`, `conversation/`) are pure *because* the quarantine holds.
28	
29	Inside that module, put **every selector and class string in one file**, and change values only
30	there (`page-adapter/selectors.js`). A selector inlined at its use site is the one that gets
31	missed when the host renames a class.
32	
33	Enforce the quarantine mechanically, by token: the repo's arch test fails if the host's class
34	prefix (`xwd__`) appears in code outside `page-adapter/`. Match against source with comments
35	**stripped** — a comment that names the token describes the code, it does not do it.
36	
37	## Identify host UI by a net, not by a selector
38	
39	A single selector is a bet that one class name survives. Cast a net instead, and make the last
40	strand semantic:
41	
42	- class nets that accept a family (`[class*="xwd__toolbar"]`), not one exact name;
43	- attribute and role hooks the host is less likely to churn (`role="cell"`, `data-testid`,
44	  `aria-label`);
45	- and a **text/shape fallback** underneath: the splash is found by class net *or* by "a visible
46	  container whose text says 'Ready to start solving' with a Play-ish button in it, whatever its
47	  classes are called" (`page-adapter/splash.js`); the pause veil is found by its copy plus
48	  visibility (`reader.js isPaused`).
49	
50	Visibility is part of identity. Hosts keep dismissed modals in the DOM, so a match that ignores
51	`display`/`visibility`/zero-size will keep reporting a splash you already cleared.
52	
53	## Write down what you verified the selectors against, and when
54	
55	The selectors file is the only place in the codebase whose truth lives on someone else's
56	server, so it carries its own provenance: the date and page it was last verified against, the
57	captured markup it was read from, and — most valuable — the **negative** findings.
58	`selectors.js` records that the state classes sit on the `<rect>` and not the `<g>`, that the
59	pencil button exposes no `aria-pressed` and no class change, that the letter/number `<text>`
60	nodes carry no distinguishing classes and the class-based selectors match nothing live. Each of
61	those is an hour of somebody's life, and none of it is recoverable from the code.
62	
63	## Ship a probe, and make a broken page a finding rather than an exception
64	
65	One entry point that reports the health of every selector against the live page —
66	`page-adapter/probe.js`, REQ-PAGE-009, run from the in-page menu (MT-01). It is the first thing
67	to run when a user says "it stopped working", and it turns "the extension is broken" into "the
68	clue-list wrapper selector matches 0, want 2".
69	
70	It must **never throw**: a probe that dies on the first missing element reports one fault and
71	hides the other nine. Collect a row per selector and return them all — and have it capture
72	forensics for the things you could *not* read (the probe here dumps the pencil button's
73	attributes precisely because its ON state has never been readable), so the next report arrives
74	with the evidence already in it.
75	
76	## Mirror the host in a fixture, and let the fixture define the expected shape
77	
78	A saved, simplified copy of the host page (`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`, served by
79	`npm run fixture`) mirrors the selectors exactly, and the integration tests drive that. It buys
80	two things a live page cannot: the read/write/watch cycle is testable in CI at all, and the
81	whole voice loop is rehearsable locally without a subscription (`npm run build:dev` widens the
82	matches to `localhost:8787`, MT-23).
83	
84	Its limit is the same as its virtue — **the fixture only ever shows you the markup you already
85	knew about**, so a passing suite is never evidence about the live page. Keep a manual-test
86	document for what only the real host can answer (`dev/docs/MANUAL-TESTS.md`), and treat every
87	live finding as a fixture update.
88	
89	## Never trust a write — verify by re-reading
90	
91	Address the target by position rather than relying on the host's own cursor conventions (click
92	each cell, then type one letter — immune to the host's advance-on-type and skip-filled
93	settings), then **read the DOM back and confirm what you meant is there** (REQ-PAGE-007). The
94	host may ignore untrusted events, may auto-advance differently than you assumed, may reject the
95	input silently; the re-read is the only thing that distinguishes those from success.
96	
97	Poll the re-read, don't do it synchronously after the last dispatch: the host renders
98	asynchronously (React here), so the DOM immediately after your event is the DOM *before* the
99	app processed it. And aim your events at a node **inside the app's own subtree** — the selected
100	element if it has focus, otherwise a known app node. A modern app delegates key handling near
101	its root, which is a descendant of `<body>`, so an event dispatched at `document` or `body`
102	bubbles *past* it and is never seen (`page-adapter/writer.js`).
103	
104	## A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one would
105	
106	The browser fills in the deprecated `keyCode`/`which`/`charCode` on every real keystroke; on
107	a synthetic one they are plain init fields that default to 0, so
108	`new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'A' })` reaches the page as a keystroke whose keyCode is
109	0. Deprecated is not the same as unread: hosts with a long-lived key-handling layer still
110	branch on the legacy fields — this one does (verified live, MT-02) — and a 0 matches nothing,
111	so the handler runs and nothing happens, indistinguishable from "the app ignores untrusted
112	events". Mirror the real event instead: `keyCode` and `which` alongside `key`/`code`,
113	`charCode` on `keypress`, and the full keydown → keypress → keyup sequence a real keystroke
114	produces (`page-adapter/writer.js` `keyEventInit`/`typeKey`).
115	
116	Build the init in **one helper** and spread it at the single dispatch site, so fidelity is one
117	function's job. That factoring is also why this rule is prose rather than a check: the init a
118	well-factored adapter dispatches is opaque to a static scan (`{ ...init }` could carry
119	anything), so a check here could only ever police code that bypasses the helper — and the
120	mistake in that code is bypassing the helper, not the field it then forgot.
121	
122	## Put back any host state you borrowed, and degrade when you cannot read it
123	
124	Driving a host toggle means driving it back: pencil mode is set to match the write and restored
125	afterwards, so the user's own typing mode is never stolen (REQ-PAGE-012).
126	
127	You will often be unable to read the state you are toggling — the live pencil button has no
128	`aria-pressed` and no class change, so "on or off?" is genuinely unanswerable. Design for the
129	unreadable case as the **normal** one, not the error case: fall back to click parity, and let
130	the feature that depends on it degrade (the letters still land; only the pencil softening is
131	lost, REQ-ANS-019) rather than failing the operation.
132	
133	## The host has a lifecycle of its own, and its blank states are not your user's doing
134	
135	You are sharing the page with an app that has its own timers, veils and modals, and each one
136	looks like something else from inside your adapter:
137	
138	- **Idle timers.** This host auto-pauses a quiet puzzle after ~30 s of no keyboard input. A
139	  voice solver touches no keyboard, so the adapter sends a bare `Shift` keydown/keyup on every
140	  heard command — a real key event that types nothing and moves nothing (REQ-LIFE-017). Choose
141	  the nudge so it cannot mutate state, and drive it from real user activity, never from a timer
142	  of your own: when the user really has gone quiet, the host *should* pause and your session
143	  should end with it.
144	- **Veils that blank the content.** The pause veil empties the visible entries. A change watcher
145	  that diffs first and checks for the veil second will read that as the user clearing the whole
146	  grid. Check for the host's own overlay states **before** diffing, report the state once, and
147	  return (`page-adapter/watcher.js`).
148	- **Pre-content splashes.** The board may not exist for minutes while a "Ready to start
149	  solving?" modal is up. Absence of the content is not absence of the app.
150	
151	## Be inert when you are off
152	
153	Your code loads on the host's page whether or not the user is using you, so **doing nothing is
154	the resting state** (REQ-NFR-004). Watchers are created on demand and stopped with the session;
155	nothing polls; nothing observes between sessions.
156	
157	Keep load-time page changes to an explicit, minimal carve-out — here exactly one: mounting the
158	toolbar button (REQ-LIFE-012). Mount it by waiting with a `MutationObserver` that **disconnects
159	the moment the element lands** (the `page-observers-disconnected` check), and give up only when
160	the host shows no app markup at all — a slow render or a splash must not cost you the button,
161	but an archive page must not leave you waiting forever.

3:Portable, project-agnostic practices for building Chrome (and Chromium) extensions — manifest versions, background/service workers, content scripts, permissions, packaging and store review — true for any extension read cold.
16:- To run a content script on arbitrary third-party pages **without** an install-time host warning, request access at runtime: declare the origins under `optional_host_permissions` plus the (silent) `scripting` permission, call `chrome.permissions.request()` **synchronously inside a real foreground user gesture** (Chrome rejects the request from a service-worker message handler), then register the script dynamically with `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts()` — never a static `content_scripts` entry. The grant can be revoked from `chrome://extensions` out from under you, so on every service-worker start reconcile your stored enabled-flag against the permission actually granted and re-register (or clean up) to match.
19:- A **registered or static content script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module.** `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode, unlike a page's `<script type="module">` or the module service worker), so a top-level `import` in one throws `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's console, not the extension's**. To load module code without a bundler, register a tiny **classic loader** whose only statement is a *dynamic* `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`: dynamic `import()` is legal in a classic script, and the module it pulls in runs in the same content-script isolated world with the content-script `chrome.*` surface intact. List that module **and its whole transitive import graph** under `web_accessible_resources` (gated to the target origins) or the fetch is blocked — and have a test walk the graph from the entry module so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list.

1	# host-page-adaptation pack (local)
2	
3	A pack for **being a guest in a web app you do not own**: reading its DOM, driving it with
4	synthetic input, watching it change, injecting your own UI into its chrome, and surviving the
5	day it is redesigned. Declared by hand as `local/host-page-adaptation` in
6	`.claudinite-checks.json`.
7	
8	**Every rule judges a DOM/API contract, not a product decision.** Each one holds for any code
9	driving a third-party page — a userscript, a browser-automation layer, an extension's content
10	script — and nothing in a rule's logic, rationale or fix text is specific to this repo. The scan
11	is repo-shape agnostic (see below), so the pack cannot pass vacuously green somewhere laid out
12	differently. This repo is where the rules were *discovered* and is the corpus they are verified
13	against; it is not what they are about.
14	
15	**Why local, not a canon declaration:** the mounted canon shelf has no home for this facet. The
16	`chrome-extension` pack covers MV3 *mechanics* — manifest, permissions, how a content script is
17	registered and why it can't be an ES module — i.e. how your code reaches the page; it says
18	nothing about what to do once it is there. `chrome-extension-release`, `node`,
19	`github-actions`, `tidy-repo`, `spec-driven-product`, `executable-requirements` and `barriers`
20	are orthogonal, and the sibling local pack `browser-speech` owns the speech surfaces, not the
21	page. Nothing here duplicates a canon rule.
22	
23	**Provenance:** distilled from this repo's real usage — the whole of
24	`extension/src/page-adapter/` (`selectors.js`, `reader.js`, `writer.js`, `watcher.js`,
25	`probe.js`, `splash.js`, `session-button.js`), the REQ-PAGE and REQ-LIFE requirement families
26	in `dev/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md`, the quarantine rule REQ-PAGE-011 and its arch test
27	(`extension-test/unit/arch.test.js`), the live-page findings recorded in `writer.js` (MT-02) and
28	in `selectors.js`'s dated verification notes, and the fake-host fixture
29	(`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`). Nothing in it is invented.
30	
31	**Promotion note:** the checks are written to be lifted as-is — repo-shape agnostic scan, DOM
32	contracts only, no project identifiers in any rule's logic or messages — so the central promote
33	stage should be able to move them into a canon pack for this facet (`host-page-adaptation`, or
34	whatever a canon `html`/DOM pack calls it) with only the `doc:` paths rewritten. The `RULES.md`
35	prose is the part still worth re-reading for project coupling at promote time: several rules
36	cite this host's specific behaviours (the ~30 s idle auto-pause, the pencil button with no
37	readable state) as evidence, and those are examples of a category, not constants.
38	
39	## Checks
40	
41	| Check | Enforces (≤5 words) | Severity |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| `page-observers-disconnected` | started DOM observers get disconnected | blocking |
44	| `synthetic-input-events-bubble` | dispatched input events set bubbles | blocking |
45	
46	**Scope.** Both scan any browser source file (`.js/.mjs/.cjs/.ts/.tsx/.jsx`) except test
47	and vendor paths — never a hard-coded project root. Each rule is gated on the DOM API it judges
48	actually appearing in the file, so the API usage *is* the trigger and the scan can be
49	repo-shaped; a path scope wired to one layout would make every rule match zero files and pass
50	vacuously green elsewhere, which is the worst failure mode a check has. The exclusion that
51	matters is test scaffolding: a test dispatching a bare event at its own jsdom node, or spinning
52	an observer it lets the runner collect, is doing something purpose-built and is not adapting to
53	a host page.
54	
55	**Parsed, not grepped, where the name alone doesn't decide it.**
56	
57	`synthetic-input-events-bubble` judges only events that are actually **dispatched** (a probe
58	event constructed to feature-detect is not input), only the interfaces that model **real user
59	input** (a `CustomEvent` is your own signal to your own listener and is legitimately
60	non-bubbling), and it resolves each side of the dispatch through **one hop**: the constructor
61	through an alias (`const Ctor = isKey ? view.KeyboardEvent : view.MouseEvent` is how a generic
62	`fire()` helper is written, and this repo's single dispatch site is exactly that shape), and
63	the dispatched value through a local (`const ev = new MouseEvent('click');
64	el.dispatchEvent(ev)` is the other shape real dispatch code takes). An init that spreads
65	(`{ ...init }`) without an explicit `bubbles:` is beyond what the rule can see, so it stays
66	silent there: the caller may well set the field, and a check that guessed would false-alarm on
67	precisely the well-factored helper that centralises this.
68	
69	**A third check was cut at review.** `synthetic-key-events-legacy-fields` (a synthetic
70	`KeyboardEvent` init must carry `keyCode`/`which`) enforced a real live-page lesson (MT-02) —
71	but this repo's only key-event construction builds its init in a helper and spreads it at the
72	one dispatch site, exactly the shape a spread-silent check can never read. A check that is
73	structurally blind to the house pattern can only ever fire on code that bypasses the `fire()`
74	helper, and the mistake in that code is the bypass, not the field it then forgot. The lesson
75	lands as prose instead (`RULES.md`, "A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one
76	would").
77	
78	`page-observers-disconnected` is deliberately **file-scoped, not flow-scoped**: proving a
79	particular observer is disconnected on every path needs real data-flow analysis, and a check
80	that guesses is worse than one that asks a simple, honest question — "this file starts an
81	observer on the page; does it anywhere disconnect one?". An observer constructed but never
82	`.observe(`d has started nothing and is not asked.
83	
84	Red-first fixtures live in `pack.test.mjs`: each rule is run against violating sources and
85	clean ones — in both the direct and the aliased-constructor form, in TypeScript under a plain
86	`src/` as well as JavaScript — and then against this repo's real `extension/src/` tree, which
87	must stay quiet. The project's vitest run picks the file up via the
88	`.claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs` include in `vitest.config.js`, so the checks ship green
89	in CI.
90	
91	**When a check's whole point is precision, red-first has to prove it in two directions.** A
92	violating fixture failing and a clean one passing only proves the shipped check is correct — it
93	says nothing about whether the parsing it does was *necessary*. So the quiet fixtures are also
94	run against the naive alternative each piece of parsing exists to avoid, and confirmed to fire
95	there: a whole-file `new …Event(` grep wrongly flags the `CustomEvent`, never-dispatched and
96	already-bubbling cases.
97	
98	## Prose (`RULES.md`)
99	
100	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
101	|---|---|
102	| quarantine host DOM in one module | prose |
103	| identify host UI by nets | prose |
104	| date what selectors were verified against | prose |
105	| probe reports, never throws | prose |
106	| mirror the host in a fixture | prose |
107	| never trust a write; re-read | prose |
108	| synthetic keystrokes carry real-event fields | prose (its bubbles half is checked) |
109	| restore borrowed host state; degrade | prose |
110	| host lifecycle states aren't user actions | prose |
111	| be inert when off | prose (its observer teardown is checked) |

Weekly **prose-to-checks** sweep over `.claudinite/local/packs` (tracking issue #160). One conversion, in `local/host-page-adaptation`. Nothing under `.claudinite/shared/` was touched.

From `host-page-adaptation/RULES.md`, "Never trust a write — verify by re-reading":

> …aim your events at a node **inside the app's own subtree** — the selected element if it has focus, otherwise a known app node. A modern app delegates key handling near its root, which is a descendant of `<body>`, so an event dispatched at `document` or `body` bubbles *past* it and is never seen.

It clears the skill's first gate (it governs how we drive a host page, not what this product renders), it is always-testable (the receiver at a `dispatchEvent` site is a static signature), and no existing check covered it: the sibling `synthetic-input-events-bubble` judges whether the event **can** travel, never **where** it is aimed. Both can be satisfied and the write still fail — `document.dispatchEvent(new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { bubbles: true }))` bubbles perfectly, past nothing.

## The check

`input-events-target-app-subtree`, **blocking**, in `local/host-page-adaptation`.

Fires when a real-input event (the `INPUT_EVENT_CLASSES` set, resolved through one constructor-alias hop and one local-variable hop, exactly as the sibling resolves it) is dispatched at a receiver written out **literally** as `document`, `document.body`, `document.documentElement`, or `window`/`globalThis`/`self` (optionally qualified, e.g. `window.document.body`).

Parsed, not grepped, and quiet in the deliberate direction:

- a target the code **resolves** — the `activeElement ?? cell ?? body` ladder a real adapter picks with — is beyond a static read, so the rule says nothing. That is why this repo's own `page-adapter/writer.js` is quiet: the mistake the rule is after is *aiming* at a global, not *falling back* to one.
- `CustomEvent` (your own signal to your own listener) and non-input events (`new Event('resize')`, which is exactly what `window` is the right target for) are never judged.

Applied to the paragraph the check now stands beside: it **stays**, untrimmed. It carries a second rule the check does not cover (poll the re-read — the host renders asynchronously, so the DOM right after your event is the DOM *before* the app processed it) and the value the check cannot judge (which node to aim at *instead*).
